items.prompt: How does a volcanic island form in the middle of the open ocean?

options.label: Floating volcanic rock drifts together and hardens into land
options.feedback: Volcanic rock does not float together and fuse on the surface; an island's rock is built in place, layer upon layer, not assembled from drifting pieces.

options.label: A meteorite impact throws up a ring of seafloor debris
options.feedback: An impact crater does not resemble the layered volcanic rock that makes up an ocean island, and most such islands show no sign of an impact at all.

options.label: Magma rises from a source on the seafloor and repeated eruptions pile up lava until it breaches the surface
options.feedback: Magma rising through a weak point in the ocean floor erupts again and again in the same spot, and each eruption adds another layer of lava on top of the last, slowly building a mountain that eventually breaks through the surface as an island.

options.label: Sediment washed off nearby continents piles up until it forms land
options.feedback: Islands rising far out in the middle of an ocean, thousands of kilometres from any continent, form with no supply of continental sediment reaching them at all.

items.ok_title: Built one eruption at a time
items.ok_line: The island is the volcano, standing tall enough to clear the water.
items.ko_line: The island's rock was made where it now stands, not gathered from somewhere else.
items.exp_title: A mountain built from repeated eruptions
items.exp_text: Where magma finds a way up through the ocean floor, it erupts and spreads as lava, which cools and hardens into a new layer of solid rock. Each further eruption from the same spot adds another layer on top of the ones before it, and over many thousands of these events the pile grows taller and taller. Once that growing pile of hardened lava finally reaches high enough, it breaks through the ocean surface and stands exposed as an island.

items.prompt: Why do some island chains, like Hawaii, form in a straight line with the islands growing progressively older toward one end?

options.label: A fixed source of magma stays in place while the ocean plate slowly drifts over it
options.feedback: A source of rising magma deep in the mantle can stay in roughly the same spot for a very long time, and as the ocean plate above it slowly drifts, a new volcano forms above the source while the older ones are carried away and slowly go extinct.

options.label: Ocean currents carry lava in a line as it erupts
options.feedback: Ocean currents move surface water, not molten rock rising up from deep inside the Earth, and they play no role in where a volcano actually forms.

options.label: Earthquakes crack the seafloor into an evenly spaced line
options.feedback: The islands in such a chain are volcanic mountains built up from repeated eruptions, not blocks of seafloor separated by cracks from a single earthquake event.

options.label: Each island was originally a single larger island that broke apart
options.feedback: The islands in such a chain formed one at a time, from separate periods of eruption, rather than starting out joined as one island and later splitting apart.

items.ok_title: The plate moves, the source does not
items.ok_line: One fixed point in the mantle, a long trail of islands left by a moving plate above it.
items.ko_title: Something is staying still while something else moves
items.ko_line: The islands get older in one direction. What could be moving relative to what?
items.exp_title: A trail left by a plate drifting over a fixed source
items.exp_text: Deep beneath the moving plates of the Earth's surface, some sources of magma called hotspots stay fixed in roughly the same place for millions of years at a time. As the ocean plate above slowly drifts across this fixed hotspot, a volcano forms and grows directly above wherever the hotspot currently sits. Once the plate's drift carries a volcano away from the hotspot, its eruptions stop and a new volcano begins forming closer to the hotspot's current position, leaving the older island behind as part of a lengthening trail.

items.prompt: How does a ring-shaped coral atoll form from what began as a volcanic island?

options.label: Coral grows on the ocean floor first, and a volcano later erupts inside the ring
options.feedback: An atoll's ring of coral begins by growing around an existing volcanic island, not the other way around; the volcano comes first and the reef develops afterward, around its edges.

options.label: Storms erode the middle of the island away, leaving only its rim
options.feedback: The middle of an atoll is missing because the old volcanic peak beneath it has sunk out of sight over a long span of time, not because storms scoured a hole out of solid rock.

options.label: The volcano explodes outward, leaving only a ring of debris
options.feedback: An atoll's ring is a living or once-living coral reef, not a scatter of rock debris from an explosive eruption, and it takes shape gradually rather than in a single blast.

options.label: Coral grows around the island's edge, and as the volcanic peak slowly sinks, the reef keeps growing upward toward the light
options.feedback: A coral reef establishes itself in the shallow water surrounding a volcanic island, and as the ageing volcano is gradually carried by the plate to cooler, lower ground and slowly subsides, the living reef keeps building upward to stay near sunlight, eventually leaving a ring of coral around a lagoon where the peak used to rise.

items.ok_line: The volcano sank. The living reef kept climbing to stay near the light.
items.ko_title: Think about which part disappears and which part keeps building
items.ko_line: The middle of the ring is missing, not added. What was there before, and where did it go?
items.exp_title: A reef that keeps pace with a sinking peak
items.exp_text: A coral reef begins growing in the shallow, sunlit water that surrounds a young volcanic island. As that volcano ages, the plate carrying it slowly moves it away from the hot region that built it, and the volcanic rock itself gradually subsides, sinking lower over a very long span of time. Because living coral can only survive near sunlight, the reef keeps building upward at roughly the same pace as the peak beneath it sinks, until eventually the volcano vanishes below the surface entirely and only the ring-shaped reef remains, encircling a lagoon.

items.prompt: Why are islands such as Great Britain considered part of a continent rather than separate volcanic peaks?

options.label: They were built by an underwater volcano near the coastline
options.feedback: These islands are made of the same continuous continental rock found on the neighbouring mainland, not layers of volcanic lava built up from an undersea eruption.

options.label: They sit on the shallow continental shelf and were joined to the mainland by dry land when sea level was lower
options.feedback: During past ice ages, so much of the world's water was locked up in ice sheets that global sea level dropped considerably, exposing the shallow continental shelf as dry land and connecting these islands to the mainland by a land bridge.

options.label: Ocean currents pushed a piece of the continent out to sea
options.feedback: Currents move water, not enormous solid blocks of continental crust, and an island like this has never physically drifted away from where it now sits.

options.label: They formed from sediment that piled up far offshore
options.feedback: These islands are made of the same solid bedrock found across the neighbouring mainland, not a heap of loose sediment that accumulated somewhere out at sea.

items.ok_title: Dry land that was later flooded
items.ok_line: The island was never separated by anything but rising water.
items.ko_title: Think about sea level, not the rock itself
items.ko_line: The rock making up the island matches the mainland exactly. What changed was not the rock, but something around it.
items.exp_title: High ground stranded by rising seas
items.exp_text: During past ice ages, enormous volumes of the world's ocean water were locked away in thick ice sheets covering much of the land, and with so much water removed from the oceans, global sea level dropped well below where it sits today. That drop exposed large stretches of the shallow continental shelf as dry land, connecting areas that are islands today directly to the neighbouring mainland by a land bridge. As the ice sheets later melted and sea level rose again, that connecting land flooded, leaving the higher ground standing above the water as a separate island.

items.prompt: Why can a violent volcanic eruption sometimes leave behind an island shaped like a curved crescent rather than a simple cone?

options.label: A powerful eruption can empty the magma chamber beneath the volcano, and the unsupported rock above collapses inward into a caldera
options.feedback: When an eruption is violent enough to expel most of the magma that had been supporting the ground above it, the rock over the now-empty chamber loses its support and collapses inward, and where part of that collapsed rim survives above the waterline, it can form a curved, crescent-shaped remnant of the original island.

options.label: Waves gradually wear an island into a crescent shape over centuries
options.feedback: Wave erosion tends to round and smooth a coastline's edges gradually rather than remove an entire section of an island at once, and a crescent island's shape traces the rim of a collapsed volcanic structure rather than a slowly eroded coast.

options.label: The island was originally two separate volcanoes that merged
options.feedback: A crescent-shaped island of this kind traces the broken rim of a single collapsed volcanic structure, not the boundary where two separate volcanoes grew together.

options.label: Coral reefs grew only along part of the original coastline
options.feedback: A crescent island of volcanic rock is shaped by the collapse of the volcano itself, not by where a coral reef happened to grow along its coast.

items.ok_title: A collapse, not a slow carving
items.ok_line: The magma chamber emptied, and the rock above had nothing left to rest on.
items.ko_title: Think about what is missing, not what wore away
items.ko_line: A crescent shape is what remains of a rim after the middle of something has dropped away.
items.exp_title: A rim left after the middle collapses
items.exp_text: A sufficiently violent eruption can expel enormous amounts of magma from the chamber beneath a volcano in a short span of time. With that magma gone, the rock that once rested above the emptied chamber loses its support and collapses downward into the space left behind, forming a large depression called a caldera. Where only part of the caldera's outer rim survives above the water afterward, the remaining island traces a curved, crescent outline rather than the shape of a complete cone.

items.prompt: Why can a newly formed volcanic island made of loose ash and cinder sometimes disappear beneath the waves again within a few decades?

options.label: Sea level rises fast enough to submerge it before it can settle
options.feedback: Global sea level does not rise nearly fast enough within a few decades to submerge a freshly built island; whatever is removing this island is acting far more quickly than that.

options.label: The island sinks straight down under its own weight
options.feedback: A freshly built pile of light volcanic ash and cinder is not especially heavy for its size, and this kind of island typically disappears from the top down through erosion, not by sinking straight downward.

options.label: Loose, unconsolidated ash and cinder have not hardened into solid rock, so ocean waves quickly wash the soft material away
options.feedback: A volcanic island built quickly from loose ash and cinder has no solid rock core holding it together, so ocean waves are able to erode and carry away that soft, crumbly material far faster than they could wear down a mountain of solid lava rock.

options.label: Fish and marine life dig burrows that collapse the island
options.feedback: A brand-new pile of volcanic ash offers little for marine life to colonise in such a short time, and the disappearance of this kind of island is driven by wave erosion of loose material, not burrowing animals.

items.ok_title: Soft material, no defence against waves
items.ok_line: Loose ash has nothing holding it together against the sea.
items.ko_title: Think about what the island is actually made of
items.ko_line: Not every volcanic island is built of the same hardened material. What is different about a very young one?
items.exp_title: An island with nothing holding it together yet
items.exp_text: A volcanic island built quickly through an eruption of ash and cinder is initially made of loose, crumbly fragments rather than a solid mass of hardened rock. Because that material has not yet cemented into anything sturdy, it offers little resistance when ocean waves repeatedly strike its shores. Without a hardened lava core to protect it, the loose material is steadily washed away, and the island can be reduced back below the waterline within a matter of decades.

items.prompt: Why can a sudden earthquake sometimes lift a stretch of seafloor above the water, creating new land?

options.label: The shaking compacts loose sediment on the seafloor until it rises
options.feedback: Compacting loose sediment would settle and lower it rather than lift it upward, and the land created this way is typically solid rock rather than compacted mud.

options.label: A sudden slip along a fault can jolt a block of crust sharply upward in an instant
options.feedback: Where two blocks of crust are pressed against a fault, built-up stress can suddenly release in a rapid slip, and that slip can jolt one block of crust upward relative to its surroundings almost instantly, exposing what had been seafloor as new land above the surface.

options.label: Tsunami waves deposit enough sand to build new land
options.feedback: A tsunami redistributes loose sand and sediment across existing land and seafloor, but this does not lift a solid block of the seafloor itself above sea level.

options.label: The earthquake heats the water enough to lower sea level locally
options.feedback: An earthquake does not release anywhere near enough heat to change the temperature or level of the surrounding ocean water in any noticeable way.

items.ok_title: A sudden jolt, not a gradual rise
items.ok_line: The block of crust does not creep upward. It jumps.
items.ko_title: Think about the crust itself, not the water or sediment around it
items.ko_line: An earthquake is a sudden release of built-up stress in solid rock. What can that kind of sudden release do to a block of crust?
items.exp_title: A block of crust jolted above the surface
items.exp_text: Along certain faults, two blocks of crust are pressed against each other under enormous built-up stress, unable to move smoothly past one another. When that stress is finally released all at once in an earthquake, one block can slip sharply relative to the other, sometimes lifting a section of the crust upward in a single sudden movement. Where that lifted block had been part of the seafloor just beneath the surface, the sudden jolt can be enough to raise it above the waterline as new land.

items.prompt: Why is the lagoon inside a coral atoll typically much shallower than the open ocean surrounding it?

options.label: The lagoon sits over the sunken top of the old volcanic cone, while the seafloor drops away steeply just beyond the reef
options.feedback: Because an atoll's lagoon occupies the space above what remains of the original volcano's upper slopes, the floor beneath it stays relatively close to the surface, while beyond the surrounding reef the seafloor plunges into the far greater depths of the open ocean.

options.label: Sand blown from nearby deserts has filled the lagoon over time
options.feedback: Atolls typically sit thousands of kilometres from any desert, and the shallow depth of a lagoon is explained by what lies directly beneath it, not by windblown sand arriving from elsewhere.

options.label: Coral reefs release gas that pushes the water outward and away
options.feedback: Living coral does not release gas that displaces or shallows the surrounding water, and the shallow depth of a lagoon has nothing to do with any gas produced by the reef.

options.label: Rainwater collecting in the lagoon raises its floor over time
options.feedback: Rainwater collecting in a lagoon adds only water, not solid material, so it cannot raise or fill in the floor of the lagoon over time.

items.ok_title: Still riding on the old volcano
items.ok_line: The lagoon floor is what is left of the mountain that used to stand there.
items.ko_title: Think about what used to be underneath the lagoon
items.ko_line: An atoll did not appear out of nothing. Something used to occupy the space where the lagoon now sits.
items.exp_title: A shallow floor left by an old mountain
items.exp_text: An atoll's ring of coral originally grew around the upper slopes of a volcanic island, and its lagoon now occupies the space directly above where that volcano's summit and upper flanks used to stand. Even after the volcanic rock has sunk well below the surface, the buried mountain beneath the lagoon keeps its floor relatively close to sea level. Just beyond the outer edge of the reef, by contrast, there is no such buried mountain holding the seafloor up, so the depth drops away far more steeply.

items.prompt: How can a thick ice sheet carve what was once solid mainland coastline into a scatter of separate islands?

options.label: The ice melts holes straight through the rock beneath it
options.feedback: Ice does not melt through solid rock from above; the deep valleys carved by glaciers are cut through the mechanical grinding of moving ice, not by the ice dissolving the rock.

options.label: Rising seas simply erode the coastline into random fragments
options.feedback: Coastal erosion by waves tends to wear a shoreline back gradually and unevenly, while the islands left by this process trace specific carved valleys rather than a random pattern of fragments.

options.label: Underground rivers hollow out tunnels that later collapse into channels
options.feedback: The deep channels separating these islands are carved directly by moving glacial ice at the surface, not by underground rivers hollowing out tunnels beneath solid rock.

options.label: A moving ice sheet grinds deep valleys into the coastal rock, and rising seas later flood those valleys, isolating the higher ground between them
options.feedback: A thick ice sheet moving across coastal terrain grinds deep, steep-sided valleys into the underlying rock, and once that ice melts away and sea level rises, seawater floods into those carved valleys, cutting off the ridges of higher ground left standing between them as separate islands.

items.ok_line: The ice cut the valleys. The sea only filled them in.
items.ko_line: Something carved deep channels into the rock long before the water that now separates these islands ever arrived.
items.exp_title: Valleys carved by ice, later filled by the sea
items.exp_text: A thick ice sheet flowing across a coastal landscape grinds and scrapes against the rock beneath and around it, wearing deep, steep-sided valleys into terrain that once stood as continuous, unbroken land. When that ice sheet eventually melts and retreats, and the ocean rises to fill the low ground it leaves behind, seawater floods into those carved valleys. The ridges of higher ground that used to stand between the valleys are left surrounded by water on every side, cut off from the mainland as separate islands.

items.prompt: How can a single volcanic event build an entirely new island out of open ocean within just a few days?

options.label: A sudden earthquake pushes an existing underwater mountain above the surface
options.feedback: This kind of rapid island is newly built from fresh volcanic material erupting at the surface, rather than an existing underwater mountain being suddenly pushed upward by shaking.

options.label: Floating pumice from a distant eruption drifts together and solidifies
options.feedback: Floating pumice scattered by a distant eruption drifts apart across the ocean surface rather than gathering together, and it does not solidify into a fixed piece of new land.

options.label: An underwater vent erupts explosively where magma meets seawater, rapidly piling ash and lava fragments into a growing cone that breaches the surface
options.feedback: When magma erupting from a vent on the seafloor meets cold seawater, the contact often triggers violent, explosive eruptions that fling huge amounts of ash and shattered lava fragments upward, and this material can pile up into a growing cone rapidly enough to break through the ocean's surface within days.

options.label: Storm waves push loose seafloor sediment into a mound above the water
options.feedback: Ordinary storm waves do not have the force needed to pile enough loose seafloor material above sea level to create new land, and this kind of rapid island-building event is driven by an eruption, not a storm.

items.ok_line: Magma meeting seawater builds fast, in ash and shattered rock rather than slow lava flows.
items.ko_line: This island appeared in days. What kind of process could pile up land that quickly?
items.exp_title: A cone built explosively in days
items.exp_text: When rising magma reaches a vent on the seafloor and meets cold seawater directly, the sudden contact often causes the eruption to become highly explosive, shattering magma into fine ash and fragments of solidified lava. These fragments are hurled upward and rain back down around the vent, piling up into a cone far more rapidly than a slow flow of lava ever could. Later flows of solid lava can then cap and cement this loose pile together, helping the new island resist being washed away again by the waves.
